challenges.name: short-lived-access-tokens-quiz
challenges.title: Expiry, units and clock skew
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence about access token expiry: the signing code behind the pentest finding, and 401 responses for learners whose phone clocks run slow.

questions.explanation: True. exp is a NumericDate, a number of seconds since the epoch (RFC 7519, section 2), but the code wrote milliseconds: 1793006100000 read as seconds is a date around the year 58,800, so exp <= now is false for every token this code ever issued. The signature only proves the API produced these claims; it says nothing about whether the claims are sensible, and here the API produced the wrong ones. Two fixes together: issue exp in seconds (iat + 900), and make the verifier reject any token whose exp - iat is larger than the maximum lifetime you issue, so a unit mistake fails loudly instead of creating immortal tokens. The misconception is that a valid signature means valid claims.

questions.question:
The web app schedules a refresh from the sign-in and refresh responses, which contain { "accessTokenExpiresAt": 1793006100 } (seconds; the access token itself is in an HttpOnly cookie):

const msLeft = body.accessTokenExpiresAt * 1000 - Date.now();
setTimeout(refreshTokens, msLeft - 60_000);   // refresh 1 minute early

Support tickets: learners whose phone clock runs about 8 minutes slow get 401 errors for several minutes before the app refreshes. API log for one of them (API servers are NTP-synchronised):

09:15:05Z GET /me/progress 401 token_expired now=1793006105 exp=1793006100 leeway=30

Statement: "Raising the API's leeway from 30 seconds to 10 minutes fixes the root cause of these 401 responses."
questions.explanation: False. The API compares exp with its own clock, which is correct; the token really is expired at 09:15:05. The root cause is in the client: it computes msLeft with the phone's Date.now(), which is 8 minutes behind, so it believes the token has 8 more minutes and schedules the refresh 8 minutes too late. Fix the client: have the server return a relative lifetime (expiresIn: 900) and schedule from the moment the response arrives, and on a 401 token_expired refresh once and retry the request. Leeway exists for small skew between the servers that issue and verify tokens (RFC 7519 allows a few minutes at most); a 10-minute leeway would also keep every stolen or revoked 15-minute token alive for 25 minutes. The misconception is that the client's clock takes part in server-side verification.

challenges.name: hs256-access-token
challenges.title: Sign and verify a short-lived access token
challenges.description: A pentest of the CodeDev API found that the hand-written access token verifier accepted a token with "alg":"none" and no signature, and tokens whose exp was written in milliseconds. Write signToken(claims, secret) and verifyToken(token, secret, options, now) for compact HS256 JWTs, using node:crypto (createHmac, timingSafeEqual) and the fake clock now, in seconds. signToken: the header is the base64url of the exact text {"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}, the payload is the base64url of JSON.stringify({ sub, iat, exp, iss, aud }) in that key order, and the signature is HMAC-SHA256 with the secret over `${header}.${payload}`, as base64url (no "=" padding); the token is header.payload.signature. verifyToken checks in this order and returns { valid: false, reason } for the first failure: "malformed" (not exactly 3 parts; a part with characters outside A-Z a-z 0-9 - _ or with length % 4 === 1; a header or payload that does not decode to a JSON object, not null and not an array); "unsupported alg" (header.alg is not exactly "HS256"); "bad signature" (the signature text differs from the expected base64url text: compare their bytes with timingSafeEqual after checking the lengths); "invalid claims" (sub not a non-empty string, iat or exp not an integer, iss not a string, aud neither a string nor an array of strings, or exp <= iat); "wrong issuer" (iss !== options.issuer); "wrong audience" (a string aud other than options.audience, or an array without it); "lifetime too long" (exp - iat > options.maxLifetimeSeconds); "expired" (now >= exp + options.leewaySeconds); "not yet valid" (iat > now + options.leewaySeconds). Otherwise return { valid: true, sub }. The test runner reads { secret, options, now, sign, verify } as JSON, signs every claims object in sign, then verifies every signed token followed by every token in verify, and prints { tokens, results }.
hints: Which parts of a token can an attacker choose freely, and which check is the first one that proves the API wrote them? Everything you decide before that check, including which algorithm to use, must not trust the token.

Look at: token.split(".") and a regular expression for the base64url alphabet (Buffer.from(text, "base64url") is lenient and silently skips characters it does not know, so test the text first); createHmac("sha256", secret).update(`${header}.${payload}`).digest("base64url") for the expected signature text; timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(a), Buffer.from(b)), which throws when the lengths differ; Number.isInteger for iat and exp.

The same rules on other input, with leewaySeconds 30 and now = 1000: exp 1000 is still valid (1000 < 1030), exp 970 is expired (1000 >= 1000); iat 1030 is valid, iat 1031 is not yet valid. The token "eyJhbGciOiJub25lIn0.e30." has three parts in the base64url alphabet (the empty signature included), its header decodes to {"alg":"none"} and its payload to {}, so it passes the format check and is rejected at the algorithm step, before any claim is read.

tests.name: Sign two tokens and verify them: one is valid, one expired 100 seconds ago
The pentest tokens: alg none without a signature, and a payload edited after signing
Clock skew: a 30-second leeway on exp and on iat, exactly at the boundaries
Issuer, audience (string or array), invalid claim types and the incident's millisecond exp
Malformed: part count, padding, + and / characters, bad lengths, non-object JSON
Algorithms and signatures: HS512, RS256, no alg, hs256, wrong key, empty or altered signature
Large input: 120 signed tokens and 200 tokens to verify, valid and attacked
